text: Quetzalcoatlus was one of the largest flying animals that ever lived. Its wings stretched about 10–11 metres from tip to tip, about as wide as a small aeroplane like a Cessna, or a little shorter than a school bus is long. When it folded its wings and walked on all fours, its head could be as high as a giraffe's, about 5 metres off the ground.
It was not a dinosaur but a [[@pterosaurs|pterosaur]], a flying reptile. It lived about 68 to 66 million years ago in what is now Texas, and it died out with the dinosaurs.

st.prompt: How do scientists think a giant like Quetzalcoatlus got off the ground?

options.t: It pushed off with its folded wings, like a pole vaulter
It ran downhill flapping, like a swan on a lake
It had to jump off cliffs every time

st.reveal: Studies of its bones suggest it crouched and used its powerful front limbs, the folded wings, to vault into the air, then flapped quickly to climb. Its arms were very strong, and this launch would have taken less than a second.

myth: Quetzalcoatlus was a flying dinosaur.

It was a pterosaur, a flying reptile that lived alongside the dinosaurs but belonged to a separate group. Its wing was a sheet of skin stretched from a hugely long fourth finger to its legs. The only flying dinosaurs were birds.

sec.t:
In 1971, a geology student named Douglas Lawson was exploring rocks in Big Bend National Park in [[@texas|Texas]]. He found part of a huge wing bone. It was clearly from a flying reptile, but it was far bigger than any known one. He named it in 1975 after Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent god of the [[@aztecs-maya|Aztecs]], who was often shown as a winged snake.

Only parts of the biggest Quetzalcoatlus have been found, mostly wing bones. Smaller relatives from the same rocks, including a second, smaller species named *Quetzalcoatlus lawsoni* and described in detail in 2021, gave scientists a better picture of its skull, neck and body. Fossils of similar giants called azhdarchids have also turned up in Romania, Jordan and elsewhere.

Flying at that size needs a very light body. Pterosaur bones were hollow, with walls sometimes only a few millimetres thick, and braced inside with thin struts, like the frame of a kite. This made them strong but very light.

Its weight is hard to work out without a full skeleton. Older studies guessed as little as 70 kg. Most researchers now think it was around 200–250 kg, about as heavy as three adult men. Its neck was over 2.5 metres long, and its head and beak alone may have been longer than a grown-up is tall.

sec.h: A giant stork, not a fishing bird
sec.t:
Old pictures showed Quetzalcoatlus skimming over the sea, scooping up fish. But its fossils come from inland areas with rivers and plains, far from the coast. Its neck was stiff, and its long, toothless beak was better for picking things up from the ground.

In 2008, palaeontologists Mark Witton and Darren Naish suggested it hunted on foot. It may have strode over the land snapping up small animals, perhaps even baby dinosaurs, rather as storks and ground hornbills do today. This idea is now widely accepted.

Quetzalcoatlus lived in the last few million years before the asteroid strike 66 million years ago. That disaster wiped out all pterosaurs, along with the non-bird dinosaurs. After that, the skies belonged to birds and, much later, bats. No flying animal since has come close to the size of the giant azhdarchids.

text: Otters live along many of India's rivers, lakes, mangroves and even paddy-field canals. There are three kinds. The smooth-coated otter is the biggest and the most common, found from the Chambal river to the Kaveri and the mangrove creeks of the Sundarbans. The Eurasian otter lives in cold Himalayan streams and in the hills of the south and Northeast.

The third is the Asian small-clawed otter, the smallest otter in the world. A grown one usually weighs less than a bag of rice. It lives in forest streams of the Western Ghats, the Northeast and the eastern coast.
Most otters are shy and busiest at dawn and dusk, so even people who fish the same river for years may only spot their tracks.

st.reveal: A family of smooth-coated otters can swim side by side in a rough line, pushing a shoal of fish towards the bank. In the shallows the fish have nowhere to escape, and everyone eats.

sec.t:
Smooth-coated otters live in families: a mother, a father and their pups from one or two years. A family can be four to a dozen strong. They sleep in a den dug into the bank, called a holt, often among tree roots.

They talk all the time. Researchers have recorded chirps, whistles, squeaks and growls, each with a different job, from "stay close" to "back off". Otters also leave messages with their droppings, called spraint, on rocks along the river. Many otter watchers in Europe say fresh Eurasian otter spraint smells oddly sweet, a bit like jasmine tea.

Small-clawed otters play a strange game. In zoos and in the wild, they juggle pebbles between their paws and mouth for no clear reason. Scientists still argue about whether it is practice, boredom or simply fun.

The [[@sundarbans-tigers|Sundarbans]] delta, shared by India and Bangladesh, is one of the best otter homes in Asia. Its [[@mangroves|mangroves]] are full of creeks where fish hide among the roots.

On the Bangladesh side, a few fishing families still keep tame smooth-coated otters on long cords. At night the otters swim under the boat and chase fish towards a net. The method is centuries old. Only a handful of families still use it, and the number keeps shrinking as fish catches fall.

All three Indian otters are now listed as threatened or near threatened worldwide. Their soft fur has been smuggled for coats for decades. Sand mining tears up the riverbanks where they dig holts. Dams cut rivers into pieces, and factory waste poisons the fish they eat.

In 2019, an international wildlife treaty called CITES gave the smooth-coated and small-clawed otters its highest protection, banning nearly all trade in them. Otters are also protected under India's wildlife law.

There is good news too. Otters need clean water with lots of fish, so seeing them means a river is fairly healthy. People have started to film otter families in city lakes and canals in several Asian cities, and in India they turn up in reservoirs and [[@wetlands|wetlands]] where few expected them. Their cousin on the Pacific coast of North America faced near wipe-out from hunters a century ago and came back. And that sea-going cousin has a trick no Indian otter needs: it holds paws with its family while it sleeps, so nobody drifts away on the waves.

text: Fuses and circuit breakers are safety guards for your home's wiring. Every wire can carry only so much electric current before it gets dangerously hot. If too much current flows, a fuse melts or a breaker switches off. That opens the circuit, the current stops, and the wires don't get hot enough to start a fire.

They step in for two main problems. One is an overload, when too many appliances run on one circuit at once. The other is a short circuit, when current finds a shortcut, perhaps through a damaged wire, and rushes through with almost nothing to slow it down.

options.t: Too much current heats it up
A tiny motor cuts it

st.reveal: Electric current heats any wire it flows through. A fuse wire is thin and made to melt at a fairly low temperature. When too much current flows, it gets hot enough to melt, opening the circuit before the thicker wires in the walls can overheat.

myth: If a fuse keeps blowing, you should put in a thicker fuse wire so it stops happening.

A fuse that keeps blowing is warning you about a real problem, such as a faulty appliance or too many things on one circuit. A thicker wire can let the walls' wiring overheat and start a fire. An electrician should find and fix the cause.

sec.t:
When current flows through a wire, it heats it. That's how a toaster or an old filament bulb works. In most wires the heat is small. But a fuse contains a deliberately thin wire that melts at a lower temperature. If the current rises too high, the fuse wire melts first and breaks the circuit.

Older Indian homes often had rewirable fuses called "kit-kat" fuses: white porcelain holders with a thin wire across them. When one blew, someone pulled it out and fitted a new piece of wire. Electrical plugs in Britain and many appliances in the USA still contain small glass or ceramic cartridge fuses. A fuse works only once, then must be replaced.

Most new homes use miniature circuit breakers, or MCBs, instead. They look like a row of small switches in the board. Inside each are two clever parts. A strip made of two different metals bends as it warms up, because one metal expands more than the other. During an overload it slowly bends far enough to flip the switch off.

The second part is a coil that acts as an electromagnet. In a short circuit, the current jumps so high that the magnet snaps the switch open almost instantly, often in about a hundredth of a second. Once the problem is fixed, you can simply push the switch back up. That is far easier than finding fuse wire with a torch during a power cut.

The two parts work at different speeds on purpose. A motor in a fridge or a mixer draws a quick surge of current when it starts, which is harmless. The slow metal strip ignores that short burst, so the breaker doesn't trip every time you make a milkshake.

{{story:electricity-history}}

Fuses and MCBs protect the wiring, but a small current through a person can still be dangerous. That's the job of an RCCB (residual current circuit breaker), sometimes called an ELCB. It constantly compares the current going out along one wire with the current coming back along the other. Normally they match exactly.

If some current goes missing, it may be leaking through faulty equipment, wet ground or someone's body. When the difference reaches a small amount, often 30 milliamps, the RCCB cuts power within a fraction of a second. In the USA, bathroom and kitchen sockets have their own version, called GFCI outlets, with little "test" and "reset" buttons on the front.

An ordinary [[@light-switch|light switch]] does something much simpler. It is a gap in a wire that you can close and open by hand. Press it one way and two metal contacts touch, completing the circuit. Press it the other way and a spring pulls them apart.

The idea of fuses goes back to the early days of [[@electricity-history|electric lighting]]. Thomas Edison patented a fuse in 1890 as part of his system for [[@electricity-home|bringing power to homes]]. Today, a switchboard is one of the quietest parts of a house. Most of the time nothing happens there at all, and that is exactly what it is for. Grown-ups should be the ones to reset a breaker, and if one keeps tripping, an electrician should check why.

text: Your brain floats inside your skull, cushioned by a thin layer of fluid. In a fall, your head can stop in a split second while your brain keeps moving and hits the inside of the skull. That is what causes concussions and worse injuries.

A helmet slows that stop down. Its hard outer shell spreads the force of a blow over a wider area and lets the helmet slide on the road instead of snagging. Underneath, a layer of stiff foam crushes as it absorbs the energy. By making your head stop over a few extra milliseconds, a helmet sharply reduces the force that reaches your [[@brain-works|brain]].

Bounces the head back like a rubber ball

st.reveal: The foam squashes as it absorbs the blow. Stretching the stop from a fraction of a millisecond to several milliseconds means much less force reaches the skull and brain.

sec.t:
A simple rule of physics is at work. The faster something stops, the bigger the force involved. Drop a glass onto a tiled floor and it shatters. Drop it onto a thick quilt and it survives, because the quilt lets it slow down gradually.

A helmet is a quilt for your head, made of foam called expanded polystyrene, or EPS. It is the same material used to pack televisions, only denser and shaped carefully. In a hard hit, millions of tiny air-filled beads in the foam collapse. That uses up the energy of the crash. Once crushed, the foam does not spring back, which is why a helmet works properly only once.

Foam that is too soft squashes flat and lets the head hit the road. Foam that is too hard barely crushes at all. Helmet makers test different densities by dropping helmets with metal heads inside and measuring the jolt.

sec.h: Helmets on Indian and American roads
sec.t:
India has more than 20 crore two-wheelers, and riders without helmets make up a large share of road deaths. Indian law requires both rider and pillion passenger to wear helmets that meet the standard IS 4151 and carry the ISI mark. The World Health Organization reports that wearing a proper motorcycle helmet cuts the risk of death by about 40% and the risk of serious head injury by about 70%.

In the USA, rules vary by state. Some require all motorcyclists to wear helmets, others only young riders. Bicycle helmets sold there must pass a federal test that involves dropping them, with a dummy head inside, onto metal anvils. Wearing a helmet is one of the simplest parts of [[@road-safety|road safety]], along with [[@seatbelts|seatbelts]] in cars.

Soldiers have worn helmets for thousands of years, from bronze helmets in ancient Greece to steel ones in the World Wars. In sport, helmets came later. Cricketers began wearing them widely in the late 1970s, when fast bowlers were hurling bouncers at well over 140 km/h. American football players wear thick helmets with face cages, and researchers are still working on ways to protect them from repeated smaller knocks.

New helmet designs add a slippery inner layer that lets the shell twist slightly on impact, reducing the twisting forces on the brain. But no helmet makes a rider invincible. It is a last line of defence, designed to matter in the one moment you hope never comes.

text: Carnatic music comes mainly from South India and Hindustani music mainly from North India. Both are built on ragas, families of notes with their own moods and rules, and on talas, repeating cycles of beats. Both use the notes Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha and Ni.

The difference is in how they are played. Carnatic music is built around fixed compositions and decorates almost every note with slides and shakes. Hindustani music gives more time to slow, open-ended exploring of a raga, often starting with no beat at all. The instruments differ too: you are likely to hear a mridangam drum in the south and a tabla in the north.

The trumpet

st.reveal: The violin reached South India around 200 years ago. Musicians played it sitting on the floor, resting it between chest and foot, and it can follow every slide of the voice.

myth: Hindustani music belongs to Muslims and Carnatic music belongs to Hindus.

Both traditions have been shaped by musicians of many faiths. Hindustani music has many Hindu musicians and devotional songs as well as famous Muslim ustads, and Carnatic music has been played and loved by people of all backgrounds.
facts: Called the father of Carnatic music

sec.t:
Both traditions grew from older Indian music, including temple songs and ancient texts. Over several centuries, North and South drifted apart. In the north, royal courts welcomed musicians from Persia and Central Asia, and new forms and instruments mixed with older Indian ones.

The emperor [[@akbar|Akbar]] gathered great musicians at his court in the 1500s, including the singer Tansen, who became a legend. In the south, music was closely tied to temples and to devotional poetry in Telugu, Tamil, Kannada and [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]]. Historians still argue about exactly when the two traditions became fully separate.

sec.h: Songs at the centre in the south

sec.t:
A Hindustani performance often begins with an *alap*, a slow, beatless introduction. The musician explores the raga note by note, as if walking slowly around a building to see it from every side. Only later does the drum join in, and the speed builds towards a fast, thrilling end.

Hindustani music also links many ragas to times of day and seasons, as you can read in [[@raga-time|ragas and time]]. Musicians learn within families of style called *gharanas*, each with its own way of singing or playing.

In the south, you will hear the [[@veena|veena]], [[@violin-india|the violin]], the flute, the barrel-shaped mridangam drum and the *ghatam*, a clay pot played as a drum. In the north, you will hear the sitar, the sarod, the bansuri flute, the [[@shehnai-bismillah|shehnai]] and the [[@tabla|tabla]].

The [[@harmonium|harmonium]], a small keyboard instrument with bellows, came from Europe in the 1800s. It became hugely popular in the north, even though All India Radio banned it from broadcasts for about 30 years, from 1940, saying it couldn't play the in-between notes of Indian music.

Today, the two traditions often share a stage. In a *jugalbandi*, a Carnatic and a Hindustani musician take turns and answer each other, playing the same raga in their own styles.

Every December, [[@chennai|Chennai]] hosts one of the biggest [[@festivals-music|music festivals]] in the world, with hundreds of Carnatic concerts across the city. Hindustani festivals, such as the Sawai Gandharva festival in [[@pune|Pune]], draw huge crowds too. In the USA, a yearly festival in Cleveland, Ohio, brings Carnatic musicians from India to American audiences.

text: The Eiffel Tower was built as the grand entrance to the 1889 World's Fair in [[@paris|Paris]], called the Exposition Universelle. That year marked 100 years since the [[@french-revolution|French Revolution]], and France wanted to show the world what modern French engineering could do.

The tower was built from wrought iron by the company of the engineer Gustave Eiffel, and at 300 metres it was by far the tallest structure in the world. It was only supposed to stand for 20 years. It was saved because scientists found it useful for experiments, especially for sending radio signals.

st.reveal: The tower is repainted by hand roughly every seven years, using around 60 tonnes of paint. The paint protects the iron from rust, the tower's biggest enemy.

myth: The people of Paris loved the Eiffel Tower from the start.
Many hated it. In 1887 a group of well-known artists and writers published a letter calling it useless and monstrous. Over time, most Parisians grew fond of it, and it became the symbol of the city.

sec.t:
In 1886 France held a competition for a centrepiece for the fair. More than a hundred designs were sent in. The winner came from Eiffel's company. Two of his engineers, Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, had first sketched the idea of a giant iron tower. The architect Stephen Sauvestre made it more elegant, adding the big arches at the base.

Gustave Eiffel was already famous for [[@bridges|iron bridges]] and for designing the iron skeleton inside the [[@statue-liberty|Statue of Liberty]] in New York.

Not everyone was impressed. In 1887, while it was being built, a group of famous artists and writers published a letter of protest. They called it useless and monstrous and said it would ruin the beauty of Paris.

When it opened, though, crowds loved it. Nearly two million people visited during the fair. People rode [[@elevators|lifts]] up the curved legs and looked out over the whole city, something few had ever done.

Eiffel's permit lasted only 20 years. After that, the city could take the tower down. Eiffel worked hard to prove it was useful. He let scientists use it for experiments in weather, air resistance and, most importantly, wireless telegraphy, sending messages by [[@radio-waves|radio waves]].

The tower was a perfect aerial, taller than anything else around. In the early 1900s the French army used it to send and receive radio messages. It was too valuable to scrap. Today it still carries antennas for radio and [[@television-invented|television]], which is why it has grown to about 330 metres.

Iron's great enemy is [[@rust|rust]], which forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water. To protect it, the tower is repainted by hand roughly every seven years, with around 60 tonnes of paint.

It has even been painted different colours over the years, from reddish-brown to yellow. From 1968 it was a bronze-brown, a little darker at the bottom and lighter at the top so the tower looked evenly coloured against the sky. The latest repainting, begun in 2019, brought back a yellow-brown that Gustave Eiffel himself chose in 1907.

The Eiffel Tower was the tallest structure in the world until 1930, when the Chrysler Building in New York overtook it. Today it is one of the most visited paid monuments on Earth, with millions of visitors a year.

Many cities have built copies of it, and its shape is so famous it can stand for Paris on a single postcard. Not bad for a building that was supposed to be temporary.

text: A clock face shows 12 hours because the day is split into two halves of 12, one for the morning and one for the afternoon and night. That gives 24 hours in total.

The habit of using 12 began in ancient [[@ancient-egypt|Egypt]], more than 3,000 years ago. The Egyptians split the night into 12 parts by watching groups of stars rise, and the daytime into 12 parts too.

Minutes and seconds come from a different place. The Babylonians, in what is now Iraq, counted in sixties. Greek astronomers later borrowed their system, and that is why an hour has 60 minutes and a minute has 60 seconds.

st.prompt: Why is 60 such a handy number for dividing an hour?

options.t: It can be split evenly into many different parts
It is the number of days in two months
It is the largest number the Babylonians knew

st.reveal: Sixty can be divided exactly by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30 and 60. So half, a third, a quarter and a fifth of an hour are all whole numbers of minutes.

n.certNote: Historians agree that the 24-hour day comes from ancient Egypt and the 60-minute hour from Babylonian maths. Why the Egyptians chose 12 in the first place is less certain, and several explanations are offered.

myth: There have always been 60 minutes in an hour, and the hours have always been the same length.
For most of history, an hour was a twelfth of the daylight, so summer hours were long and winter hours short. Equal hours became normal only once mechanical clocks spread in the 1300s and later.
facts: ancient Egypt, using groups of stars

sec.t:
On clear desert nights, Egyptian priests watched the sky. They picked out 36 groups of stars, now called decans, that rose one after another through the year.

On any given night about 12 of these groups rose between dusk and dawn. So the night was divided into 12 parts. Sundials then split the daylight into parts as well, and in time the day had 12 hours too.

Those hours were not all the same length. A summer night's hours were short and a winter night's hours were long, because each one was simply a twelfth of the dark.

Most of us count in tens, probably because we have ten fingers. The people of [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] counted in sixties instead, a system called sexagesimal.

Sixty is a very friendly number. It can be divided exactly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30. That makes sharing easy, with no awkward fractions. The same reason explains why 12 is useful: you can split it into halves, thirds, quarters and sixths.

Some people think counting by twelves came from fingers too. Touch your thumb to the three sections on each of your other four fingers and you get exactly 12.

{{story:constellations}}

Ancient India had its own way to divide the day. A full day and night held 60 ghatis, each about 24 minutes long. Each ghati was split again into 60 smaller parts called palas.

People measured ghatis with a water clock. A small bowl with a hole in the bottom was floated in a bigger pot of water. It slowly filled and sank, marking one ghati each time. Some temples and royal courts kept these water clocks running all day. You can still find ghatis in traditional [[@indian-calendars|Indian calendars]].

With two sets of 12 hours, you need a way to tell them apart. English uses a.m. and p.m., short for the Latin words ante meridiem and post meridiem. They mean "before midday" and "after midday".

The [[meridian|meridian]] here is the line in the sky the Sun crosses at noon, when it is highest. That is why noon itself is the confusing case. It is neither before nor after midday, so some people write "12 noon" just to be clear.

In 1793, during the French Revolution, France tried to make time decimal like its new metric system. A day had 10 hours, each of 100 minutes, each of 100 seconds. Clockmakers built special faces for it. But people were used to the old hours, and France gave up decimal time within about two years.

Today many places use a 24-hour clock. [[@indian-railways|Indian Railways]], airlines and armies all write times like 18:30 instead of 6:30 p.m., because it avoids mixing up morning and evening. Most kitchen [[@clocks|clocks]] still show 12, a habit Egyptian stargazers started long ago.

text: Simone Biles is an American [[@gymnastics|gymnast]] and the most decorated gymnast in history. By 2024 she had won 11 Olympic medals, seven of them gold, and 30 World Championship medals. She does skills so difficult that few other women even try them, and several are named after her.

She is also famous for something braver than any flip. In 2021 she stepped back from most events at the Tokyo Olympics to protect her safety and mental health. Three years later she came back and won three gold medals in Paris.

st.reveal: Gymnasts call it "the twisties". Her brain and body stopped agreeing about where she was mid-flip, which can cause dangerous landings. She stepped back to stay safe, and came back to win a bronze on the beam later in the Games.

myth: Being small makes gymnastics easy.
A short body spins faster, which helps with flips, but it still needs huge strength. Biles can lift and launch her own body weight with power that many much bigger athletes cannot match.

sec.h: A hard start and a new home
sec.t:
Biles was born in Columbus, Ohio, in 1997. As a small child she spent time in foster care. Her grandparents, Ron and Nellie Biles, later adopted her and her younger sister, and raised them near Houston in [[@texas|Texas]]. She calls them Mum and Dad.

At six, on a day-care trip to a gym, she copied the older gymnasts. A coach sent a letter home suggesting she join a class. She trained with one coach, Aimee Boorman, for many years.

At her first Olympics, in Rio de Janeiro in 2016, Biles won four golds: team, all-around, vault and floor. She also won bronze on the beam. She was 19 and became famous around the world almost overnight.

Her floor routines were full of energy and jokes. Judges and fans could see she loved performing. She was chosen to carry the US flag at the closing ceremony.

Gymnastics scoring changed in 2006. Instead of a perfect 10, each routine now gets a difficulty score plus an execution score. That lets a gymnast like Biles gain extra points by trying harder skills, if she can land them cleanly.

At the Tokyo Olympics, held in 2021, Biles was expected to win many golds. During the team final she lost her sense of where she was in the air, a problem gymnasts call "the twisties". In a sport where a bad landing can break a neck, that is dangerous.

She withdrew from several events. Some people criticised her, but many athletes and doctors praised her for putting safety first. She returned to win bronze on the beam. Her decision started a worldwide conversation about athletes' [[@mental-health|mental health]].

In Paris in 2024 Biles won gold in the team event, the all-around and the vault, and silver on the floor. She was 27, old for a top gymnast. She has said therapy helped her return.

Biles has also spoken out to protect young athletes, after the team doctor of USA Gymnastics was jailed for abusing many gymnasts, including her. She wants children in sport to feel safe and to be heard. In 2023 she married the American football player Jonathan Owens, and she still trains at a gym her family owns near Houston.

text: Colour blindness means seeing colours differently from most people, usually by mixing up certain shades. It's not really blindness. Most colour-blind people see many colours, but some pairs, such as red and green, or brown and green, look alike to them.

It happens because of the cells in the [[retina|retina]] that sense colour, called cones. Most people have three kinds, tuned roughly to red, green and blue light. The brain compares their signals to work out every colour. In colour blindness, one kind of cone works differently or is missing, so some colours become hard to tell apart.

st.prompt: Why is red-green colour blindness much more common in boys than in girls?

options.t: The gene involved sits on the X chromosome, and boys have only one X
Boys' eyes are bigger, so colours spread out more
Girls practise naming colours more when young

st.reveal: Boys have one X chromosome and girls have two. If a boy's X carries the colour gene change, nothing backs it up. A girl usually has a working copy on her other X, so she sees colours normally.

That's extremely rare. Most colour-blind people see plenty of colours but confuse certain ones, usually reds, greens, browns and oranges.

sec.t:
Among people of northern European descent, about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have red-green colour blindness. Rates differ between populations, and studies in India generally report somewhat lower figures, but in almost every country it's far more common in boys.

The reason lies in [[@genes-family|genes]]. The instructions for red and green cones sit on the X [[chromosome|chromosome]]. Boys have one X and one Y, while girls have two X's. If a boy's X carries the change, he will be colour blind. A girl needs the change on both X's, which is much rarer.

John Dalton, the English chemist famous for his ideas about atoms, noticed something odd about himself. A geranium flower that looked sky-blue to him in daylight looked red by candlelight, though most people saw it as pink all along. His brother saw colours the same way.

In 1794 he described this to a scientific society in Manchester. It was one of the first careful scientific accounts of colour blindness, which became known as Daltonism. Dalton wanted his eyes examined after his death to test his theory about them. They were kept in a jar for more than 150 years. In 1995, scientists extracted DNA and showed he was missing the green-sensing cone.

Many colour-blind people only find out when they mix up colours in art class or at a test. Small things can cause trouble: telling ripe fruit from unripe, reading charts, or knowing whether meat is cooked.

There are clever workarounds. [[@traffic-lights|Traffic lights]] always keep red at the top and green at the bottom, so drivers can go by position. Good designers add patterns or labels to maps and graphs instead of relying on colour alone. Phones and computers now offer colour filters, one of many tools in [[@accessibility-tech|accessible technology]]. Special glasses can help some people tell certain colours apart better, though they don't restore normal colour vision.

Many mammals, including dogs and cats, have only two kinds of cones. Dogs see blues and yellows well but find reds and greens hard to tell apart, much like a person with red-green colour blindness. Many birds and insects, on the other hand, can see [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light, a colour completely invisible to us.

text: Usually a little, yes. Many studies have found that people who regularly notice what they're thankful for feel slightly happier and more satisfied with their lives. Some also sleep a bit better and feel closer to friends and family.

The key word is "slightly". Gratitude is not a magic switch. Larger reviews of the research suggest the boost is real but modest, and it works better for some people than others. It also can't fix big problems on its own. If you feel low for a long time, talking to a trusted adult or a doctor matters far more than any thank-you list.

st.reveal: The gratitude group felt more positive about their lives and even said they exercised more. The difference was not huge, but it showed up clearly against the other two groups.

myth: Being grateful means pretending everything is fine.
You can feel grateful and sad, worried or angry at the same time. Gratitude is about noticing the good things too, not hiding the hard ones.

sec.h: The study that started a craze
sec.t:
In 2003 two American psychologists, Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough, split college students into three groups. Every week for ten weeks, one group wrote down up to five things they were grateful for. Another wrote down hassles, like traffic or a messy room. The third simply wrote down events.

At the end, the gratitude group felt better about their lives and more hopeful about the coming week than the hassles group. They even reported fewer aches and more exercise. The study became famous, and "gratitude journals" took off around the world. Shops now sell notebooks with a printed space for each day's thanks. Other scientists have since tested the idea many times, with mixed but mostly positive results.

In another experiment, people wrote a letter to someone who had helped them but whom they had never properly thanked. Then they visited and read it aloud. Their happiness rose sharply, and in that study the effect lasted about a month.

Many writers are surprised by how nervous they feel before reading the letter, and how glad the other person is to hear it. People tend to underestimate how much a sincere thank-you means to someone else.

Gratitude exercises don't suit everyone, though. In one study, people who counted their blessings once a week felt better than people who did it three times a week, perhaps because the habit stayed fresh. Some people feel guilty when told to be grateful, as if they aren't allowed to be upset. Psychologists warn against telling someone who is hurting to "just be thankful". That can leave them feeling unheard.

Many cultures build thankfulness into the calendar. In the USA, [[@thanksgiving|Thanksgiving]] began as a harvest celebration and is now a day for family meals. Harvest festivals such as Pongal in Tamil Nadu thank the sun, the rain and the cattle that helped the crops grow.

Many religions build thanks into daily life too, through prayers before meals, morning prayers and offerings from the first harvest, in Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Sikh and Jewish traditions, among others.

Customs differ, though. In some Indian families, saying "thank you" to parents or siblings can sound oddly formal, because helping is simply expected. Gratitude there shows up as a touch of the feet, a favourite dish cooked, or a cup of chai brought without asking. Scientists mostly study written lists, but those everyday habits may count just as much.

text: Your ears can be damaged by sounds that are too loud, or by fairly loud sounds that go on for too long. The damage happens in the [[cochlea|cochlea]], a snail-shaped tube deep inside each ear. It's lined with rows of tiny hair cells that bend when sound waves pass, sending signals to the brain.

Very loud noise can bend these hair cells so hard that they are injured or die. In humans they don't grow back, so the hearing loss is permanent. The good news is that noise damage is almost completely preventable by turning volume down, taking breaks and protecting your ears around very loud sounds.

myth: If loud music doesn't hurt, it can't be damaging your ears.

sec.t:
Loudness is measured in [[decibel|decibels]], or dB. A whisper is about 30 dB, normal talking about 60 dB, and heavy city traffic about 85 dB. A rock concert can reach 110 dB, and a big firecracker exploding nearby can be louder still.

The scale is tricky. Each 10 dB step means ten times more sound energy. So 100 dB isn't just a bit louder than 90 dB. It carries ten times as much energy, and it can damage ears in a fraction of the time.

The World Health Organization suggests children keep their weekly listening at around 75 dB or lower. The louder a sound, the shorter the safe time.

Earphones send sound straight into the ear canal, so it's easy to turn them up too high without realising, especially on a noisy bus or Mumbai local train. The WHO estimated in 2022 that over a billion young people worldwide are at risk of hearing loss from unsafe listening habits.

Many phones now warn you when the volume has been high for a long time. A simple rule of thumb many audiologists suggest is to keep the volume below about 60% and take regular breaks. [[@how-headphones|Headphones]] with [[@noise-cancelling|noise cancelling]] can help, because blocking outside noise means you don't need to turn the music up as much.

Festivals can be loud in both India and the USA, from Diwali and wedding processions to Fourth of July fireworks and packed football stadiums. Indian rules set noise limits for firecrackers and for [[@loudspeakers|loudspeakers]] at night, though they are not always followed.

Standing further from loudspeakers, covering your ears during big bangs, and wearing soft foam [[@how-noise-cancel-ears|earplugs]] at concerts all protect your hearing. Workers in noisy factories and on airport runways wear ear defenders for the same reason.

If someone has trouble hearing, a hearing test is quick and painless. [[@hearing-aids|Hearing aids]] make sounds louder, and cochlear implants can send signals directly to the hearing nerve for people with severe loss. Many deaf people also communicate in [[@sign-language|sign language]], a full language with its own grammar. Tell an adult if your ears ring often or sounds seem muffled for more than a day.

text: Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps [[@blood|blood]] around your body roughly 1 lakh times a day, carrying oxygen and food to every cell.

Keeping it healthy is mostly about everyday habits. Move your body every day, eat plenty of fruit, vegetables, pulses and whole grains, go easy on salty snacks and sugary drinks, get enough sleep and never start smoking. For most children, the heart is strong and healthy. The point of good habits is to keep it that way for the next 80 years.

At least 15 minutes

st.reveal: WHO suggests an average of at least 60 minutes a day of moderate to vigorous activity, the kind that makes you breathe harder. It can be split up, so a cycle to school, a game at break and a dance in the evening all count.

myth: Heart disease is only something old people need to worry about.

Heart attacks are much rarer in the young, but the narrowing of arteries can begin in childhood and builds up over decades. Habits formed early, like being active and not smoking, make a big difference later.

sec.t:
Each heartbeat squeezes blood out into a network of tubes. Arteries carry it away from the heart, veins bring it back, and tiny [[capillary|capillaries]] connect the two. Laid end to end, an adult's blood vessels would stretch for tens of thousands of kilometres.

Like any muscle, the heart gets stronger with use. When you run, cycle or play football, your heart beats faster to deliver more oxygen, as explained in [[@heartbeat-exercise|heartbeat and exercise]]. Over weeks and months, regular exercise makes the heart pump more blood with each beat. That is why trained athletes often have a slower resting pulse than other people.

No single food is magic, but some patterns help. Diets with plenty of vegetables, fruit, dal, beans, nuts and whole grains are linked to healthier hearts.

Too much [[@salt|salt]] can raise blood pressure over time, which strains the heart and blood vessels. Much of the salt people eat hides in packaged snacks, [[@maggi-noodles|instant noodles]], pickles and fast food, not just the salt shaker. Sugary drinks and lots of fried [[@junk-food|junk food]] can lead to weight gain and other changes that are hard on the heart.

Sleep gives the heart a break, because your heart rate and blood pressure drop at night. Children aged 6 to 12 generally need 9 to 12 hours. Long hours sitting still in front of screens, without breaks, mean less exercise and often more snacking.

Feeling worried or stressed now and then is normal. Ongoing stress can affect sleep and eating, though, so talking to a parent, teacher or friend about worries is good for your whole body.

sec.h: Heart health in India and the USA
sec.t:
Heart disease is a leading cause of death in both India and the United States. Studies suggest people of South Asian origin, in India and abroad, tend to develop heart disease at younger ages than many other groups. Doctors think genes, diet and lifestyle all play a part.

Both countries run campaigns to cut smoking and salt, and to get children moving. If you have questions about your own heart, such as a racing heartbeat when you are resting or chest pain, tell a parent and see a doctor. Most of the time it turns out to be nothing serious, but it's always worth checking.

text: Computers only store numbers, so every letter, digit and symbol has to be given a number. Unicode is one giant agreed list that gives a unique number to every character in almost every written language. The English A is 65. The Hindi क is 2,325. The Tamil அ, the Chinese 水 and the 😀 emoji each have their own.

Because every phone, laptop and website uses the same list, a message typed in Kolkata in Bengali arrives in Kansas as Bengali. Without it, the receiving computer might show nonsense or empty boxes. As of version 17.0 in 2025, Unicode holds 159,801 characters from more than 170 scripts.

st.prompt: In the computer codes most systems still use, what number stands for a capital A?
st.reveal: The old ASCII code, from the 1960s, gave capital A the number 65, B 66 and so on. Unicode kept those numbers, so old English text still works, and then added thousands more for other scripts.

Unicode decides each emoji's number and meaning, such as "grinning face". Apple, Google, Samsung and others then draw their own pictures, so the same emoji can look a little different.
facts: Unicode, run by the Unicode Consortium

sec.t:
In the 1960s American engineers agreed on a code called ASCII. It had 128 slots: English letters, numbers, punctuation and some controls. That was fine for English. It had no room for é, ñ, क or 漢.

So every country and company made its own extra codes, and they clashed. The same number might mean a Russian letter on one computer and a Greek one on another. Emails turned into rows of question marks. Indian newspapers in the 1990s each used their own font codes, so a page typed for one couldn't be read with another. Japanese even has a word, mojibake, for the scrambled text this caused.

The Unicode Consortium is a non-profit group based in California. Its members include tech companies, universities and some governments. Anyone can propose a new script or character, but they need evidence that people really use it, along with a careful description of how its letters behave.

That matters for small languages. Once a script is in Unicode, people can text, search and publish in it. Santali's Ol Chiki script, from eastern India, was added in 2008. In 2025 Unicode added Tolong Siki, a script created in the 1990s for the Kurukh language of Jharkhand and nearby states. For [[@endangered-languages|endangered languages]], getting onto phones can help young people keep writing them.

Unicode also covers scripts nobody writes any more. Egyptian hieroglyphs, Brahmi, the script of Emperor Ashoka's edicts, and cuneiform from ancient Mesopotamia all have their own blocks of numbers. That lets historians type, search and share ancient texts as easily as a text message.

sec.h: Emoji and the rules of joining
sec.t:
[[@emojis|Emoji]] started on Japanese mobile phones in the late 1990s. In 2010 they joined Unicode, which is why they now work across the world. New emoji are approved each year, after people send in proposals.

Numbers alone are not enough, though. Indian scripts join letters into new shapes, and Arabic letters change form depending on their neighbours. Unicode stores the plain letters in order. The font and the phone's software then work out the right shapes on screen, which is why [[@keyboards-languages|typing in Hindi or Tamil]] looks right even though you pressed separate keys. The list keeps growing, one carefully checked character at a time.

text: Gobekli Tepe was built by hunter-gatherers, people who lived by hunting wild animals and gathering wild plants. They lived in what is now south-eastern Türkiye about 11,500 years ago, and they had no metal, no wheel and no writing.

Even so, they dug round enclosures and set up huge T-shaped stone pillars, some about 5.5 m tall and weighing several tonnes. They carved them with foxes, boars, snakes, scorpions and vultures. Gobekli Tepe is older than [[@stonehenge|Stonehenge]] by about 6,000 years. Nobody knows its original name. *Göbekli Tepe* is Turkish for "Hill of the Navel" or "Potbelly Hill".

st.reveal: They carved the pillars with stone tools, probably flint. Metal tools wouldn't arrive in the region for thousands of years. They had fire, rope and lots of teamwork.

myth: Gobekli Tepe is so old and so big that it must have been built by a lost advanced civilisation.
There is no evidence of any lost civilisation. Tools, food waste and bones found at the site show it was built by local hunter-gatherers using stone tools, rope and a lot of people working together.

sec.h: A hill that hid a secret
sec.t:
In the 1960s, researchers surveying the area noticed broken pieces of stone on the hill and thought it was a medieval graveyard. Farmers ploughed around big stones for years.

In 1994, the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt looked again and realised the stones were much older. From 1995, his team began to dig. They found circle after circle of pillars, buried under soil. Radar scans show there are more enclosures still underground. Only a small part has been dug.

Klaus Schmidt thought Gobekli Tepe was a temple, a place people came to for feasts and ceremonies but didn't live in. He called it "the first temple". He believed hunters gathered from far away to build it, and feasted on gazelle meat and something like beer as they worked.

Since Schmidt died in 2014, other archaeologists have kept digging. They found water channels, rainwater cisterns, houses and huge numbers of grinding stones. Now many think people did live there, at least part of the time. It may have been a village with special buildings, a bit like a town with a big temple at its heart.

Either way, the work needed hundreds of people to plan, quarry, carve and move stones. Something brought them together.

sec.h: Did a temple lead to farms
sec.t:
Here is the big idea. Wild wheat grew on hills nearby, and genetic studies show that one of the earliest kinds of farmed wheat came from this region. Some archaeologists think the need to feed crowds of builders pushed people to plant and look after wild grains. If so, building Gobekli Tepe may have helped kick-start [[@farming-began|farming]].

Other experts think farming and big buildings grew up together, each pushing the other. Either way, Gobekli Tepe turned an old belief upside down. People used to think farming came first, then villages, then temples. Here, the giant stones came very early.

Around 8000 BCE, the site was given up, and its enclosures filled with soil. Nearby, a similar site called Karahan Tepe is now being dug. Its carvings include human heads and snakes, and it may be just as old. On the Gobekli pillars, vultures appear again and again. These birds still soar over the region, and they were once common in India too, where [[@vultures-india|vultures]] have played their own part in burials and beliefs.

text: The Salt March was a protest led by Mahatma [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] in 1930 against the British salt law. Under the Salt Act of 1882, Indians were not allowed to make or sell their own [[@salt|salt]]. They had to buy salt that was taxed by the government.

On 12 March 1930, Gandhi and 78 followers set out from his Sabarmati Ashram in [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]]. They walked about 385 km in 24 days to the village of Dandi on the coast of Gujarat. On 6 April, Gandhi picked up a lump of natural salt from the shore, breaking the law. Across India, people began making salt, selling it and refusing to obey. Tens of thousands were arrested, and newspapers around the world reported the protest.

st.prompt: Why did Gandhi pick salt as the law to break?

options.t: Everyone needs salt, so the tax hurt rich and poor alike
Salt was the most expensive thing in India
The British had banned eating salt

st.reveal: Under the Salt Act, Indians could not make or sell their own salt, and had to buy taxed salt. Since everyone needs salt, the law touched every family. Breaking it was simple, since anyone near the sea could make salt by letting seawater dry in the sun.

d.try: With an adult, dissolve two spoons of salt in a cup of warm water. Pour a little into a shallow dish and leave it in a sunny window for a few days. As the water evaporates, salt crystals will appear, just like the salt Gandhi and the marchers made by the sea.
myth: The Salt March forced the British to scrap the salt tax straight away.
The Salt Act stayed. A deal in 1931 allowed people living near the coast to make salt for their own use, but the salt tax was not abolished until shortly before independence.

sec.t:
Many of Gandhi's colleagues were puzzled when he chose salt. They expected a protest about land taxes or government power.

But Gandhi saw that salt touched everyone. A poor farmer in the heat needs salt just as much as a rich merchant. In a country with a long coastline, salt could be made for almost nothing by drying seawater in the sun. Making it a crime and taxing it showed clearly how unfair foreign rule was. Anyone, anywhere near the sea, could join the protest just by making a handful of salt.

On the morning of 6 April 1930, after prayers and a dip in the sea, Gandhi bent down and picked up a lump of salty mud. It was a tiny act, but it broke the law in front of the world.

Within days, people all along India's coasts were [[@boiling-water|boiling]] seawater and making salt. In towns far from the sea, people sold salt in public and boycotted British cloth and liquor shops. Women joined in huge numbers, picketing shops and leading marches.

On 5 May, Gandhi was arrested. The poet and leader [[@sarojini-naidu|Sarojini Naidu]] then led a peaceful raid on the Dharasana salt works.

Row after row of marchers walked forward and were struck down by police with steel-tipped lathis, without lifting a hand to defend themselves. The American journalist Webb Miller watched and wrote about it. His report appeared in hundreds of [[@newspapers|newspapers]] around the world, and turned many people abroad against British rule in India.

The salt law did not end at once. But in 1931, the Gandhi–Irwin Pact released prisoners and let coastal villagers make salt for their own use. Gandhi went to London for talks on India's future.

More importantly, the march showed that non-violent protest could move a whole nation. Decades later, Gandhi's methods guided the marches of [[@martin-luther-king|Martin Luther King Jr.]] in the USA. Today a memorial at Dandi shows the marchers in bronze, walking towards the sea.

text: A capital city is the place where a country's or state's government is based. It is usually where the parliament meets, where the president, prime minister or king has an official home, and where the top court sits. Embassies of other countries cluster there too.

The word comes from the Latin "caput", meaning head, because a capital is the head of a country's government. India's capital is New Delhi. The United States' capital is Washington, DC. Each Indian state and each US state also has its own capital, where its own assembly or legislature meets. Some capitals are ancient cities that grew important over centuries. Others were planned on empty land and built for the job.

st.prompt: One Indian city is the capital of two different states at the same time. Which is it?

options.t: Chandigarh
Hyderabad
Shimla

st.reveal: Chandigarh is the capital of both Punjab and Haryana, and is itself a union territory run by the central government. Hyderabad was a shared capital of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh for ten years after 2014, but that arrangement has ended.

myth: A country's capital is always its biggest city.
Often it isn't. Washington, DC, is much smaller than New York, Canberra is smaller than Sydney, Ottawa is smaller than Toronto, and Brasília is smaller than São Paulo.

sec.t:
During much of British rule, Calcutta (now [[@kolkata|Kolkata]]) was the capital of British India. In 1911, at a grand ceremony called the Delhi Durbar, King George V announced that the capital would move to Delhi. Delhi had been the seat of powerful rulers for centuries, from the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] to the [[@mughals|Mughals]], as told in [[@delhi|Delhi]].

The architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker designed a new city beside old Delhi. New Delhi was inaugurated in 1931. Its broad avenues lead to Rashtrapati Bhavan, the President's house, and close by stands [[@lok-sabha-rajya-sabha|Parliament]], where India's laws are made.

Some countries split their capital's jobs. [[@south-africa|South Africa]] has three: Pretoria for the government, [[@world-cape-town|Cape Town]] for parliament, and Bloemfontein for the top appeals court. Bolivia's government sits in [[@extreme-highest-city|La Paz]], while its constitution names Sucre as the capital.

In the Netherlands, Amsterdam is the official capital, but the government and parliament work in The Hague. In British India, the government moved up to [[@himachal|Shimla]] in the hills every summer to escape the heat of the plains, making it a summer capital.

Every Indian state has its own capital, from Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala to Itanagar in Arunachal Pradesh. [[@chandigarh|Chandigarh]], designed by the Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier in the 1950s, was planned as a modern city with numbered sectors, gardens and lakes. It serves as capital for both Punjab and Haryana, a story connected to how [[@states-india|India's states]] were drawn.

US state capitals are often not their state's biggest city either. The capital of New York State is Albany, not New York City. California's is Sacramento, not Los Angeles.

Rulers often chose capitals for safety, for trade or to unite a country. Some capitals sit on rivers or coasts for easy travel. Others were placed in the centre to be fair to all regions.

Countries still move capitals today. Indonesia has been building a new capital on the island of Borneo, partly because Jakarta is crowded and parts of it are sinking.

text: Aesop is the name attached to hundreds of short animal stories, called [[fable|fables]], that end with a lesson. The Tortoise and the Hare, The Fox and the Grapes, and The Boy Who Cried Wolf are all said to be his.

Ancient Greek writers believed Aesop was a real man who lived around 600 BCE. The historian Herodotus, writing more than a century later, says he was enslaved on the island of Samos. Beyond that, his life is a mix of history and legend. Some scholars think "Aesop" became a handy name for any old fable, the way many Indian jokes get pinned on Birbal.

st.prompt: In the fable, a thirsty crow drops pebbles into a jug until the water rises high enough to drink. When scientists tested real birds, what happened?

options.t: Some birds dropped stones in to raise the water and reach a treat
No bird ever worked it out
The birds tipped the jug over instead

st.reveal: In experiments, rooks and New Caledonian crows dropped stones into tubes of water to bring a floating snack within reach. They also learned that heavy stones worked better than light ones. The old fable got the bird right.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Aesop.
Herodotus, Histories, Book 2.
n.certNote: Greek writers from the 400s BCE mention Aesop as a real person, but no writing by him survives. Historians are unsure how much of his life story is true, and many fables carrying his name were added much later.

myth: Aesop wrote down all the fables we call Aesop's Fables.
Nothing written by Aesop survives, and he may have told his stories only aloud. The fables were collected centuries after his time, and later writers added hundreds more.

sec.h: A storyteller without a voice of his own
sec.t:
According to the stories told about him, Aesop was born into slavery and won his freedom through his wit. In [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]], many households and workshops depended on enslaved people, who had few rights. A clever story was a safe way to make a point about the powerful without naming them.

A later "Life of Aesop", written hundreds of years after his death, describes him as ugly but brilliant, outwitting his master and arguing with kings. Historians treat this book as entertainment rather than fact. It does show what people wanted Aesop to be: proof that wisdom could come from someone with no power at all.

A fable is short. It usually has animals that talk and act like people, a single problem, and a twist. The fox can't reach the grapes, so he decides they were sour anyway. That is where the phrase "sour grapes" comes from.

The lesson, or moral, is often added as a final line. In many cases that line was written by later collectors, not by the original teller. Different versions sometimes draw different morals from the same tale. In The Boy Who Cried Wolf, a shepherd boy keeps shouting "Wolf!" for fun. When a real wolf comes, nobody believes him. The lesson, that liars are not believed even when they tell the truth, needs no explaining.

Animal stories with lessons appear in [[@myths-african|many cultures]]. India's [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]] and the Buddhist [[@jataka-tales|Jataka tales]] are full of them, and a few plots look very similar to Aesop's. Scholars still debate whether stories travelled along trade routes or grew up separately in different places.

{{story:crow-smart}}

sec.h: From Greece to the printing press
sec.t:
The first known collection of Aesop's fables was made around 300 BCE by Demetrius of Phalerum, but it is lost. The Roman poet Phaedrus later turned many fables into Latin verse. Copies were made by hand for over a thousand years.

When the [[@printing-press|printing press]] arrived in Europe, Aesop became one of the first bestsellers. William Caxton printed an English [[@translation|translation]] in 1484. Since then, Aesop has been used in schools around the world to teach reading. Indian children often meet him in the same books as the Panchatantra. The tales are so short that teachers can read one aloud in a minute, and so clear that a six-year-old can explain the lesson back.

Some fables describe real animal behaviour. In the 2000s, scientists in England gave rooks a tube of water with a worm floating out of reach. The birds dropped stones in to raise the level. Later studies found [[@crow-smart|crows]] doing the same. A story told in Greece 2,500 years ago turned out to be a fair test of bird intelligence.

text: *Charlotte's Web* is a children's novel by the American writer E. B. White, published in 1952 with drawings by Garth Williams. It tells the story of Wilbur, a pig on a farm, and Charlotte, a grey barn spider who becomes his best friend.

When Wilbur learns he is going to be killed for meat at Christmas, Charlotte comes up with a plan. She weaves words into her web above his pen, starting with "SOME PIG". People flock to see the miracle pig, and Wilbur becomes too famous to kill.
The book is about [[@friendship|friendship]], loyalty and the turning of the seasons. It is also about death, handled honestly and gently, which is one reason so many readers remember it for life.

st.prompt: Charlotte is a spider. How many legs does she have, and what kind of animal is she?

options.t: Eight legs, an arachnid
Six legs, an insect
Eight legs, an insect

st.reveal: Spiders have eight legs and two main body parts, so they are arachnids, like scorpions and ticks. Insects have six legs and three body parts. In the book, Charlotte eats insects, such as flies, that get caught in her web.

Spiders are arachnids, not insects. They have eight legs instead of six, no wings or antennae, and their bodies have two main parts instead of three.

sec.h: Fern, Wilbur and a talking barn
sec.t:
The story begins when Fern Arable, an eight-year-old girl, stops her father from killing the runt of a litter of piglets. She names him Wilbur and raises him with a bottle. When he grows too big, he goes to live in her uncle's barn.

The barn is full of talking animals: geese, sheep, an old rat named Templeton who cares mostly about food, and, high in a corner of the doorway, Charlotte. At first Wilbur thinks she is cruel, because she catches and eats flies. Then he discovers how kind and clever she is.

Charlotte writes "SOME PIG", then "TERRIFIC", "RADIANT" and "HUMBLE". Templeton, grumbling, fetches words from old newspapers for her to copy.

{{story:spiders-silk}}

E. B. White lived on a farm in Maine, in the north-east of the USA. He kept pigs, geese and sheep, and he spent a lot of time watching a big grey spider spin her web in his barn.

White was famous for writing for *The New Yorker* magazine, and he did careful research. He read books about spiders and checked facts with experts. Charlotte's full name, Charlotte A. Cavatica, comes from the scientific name of the barn spider, *Araneus cavaticus*.

He once cut down a real egg sac and took it back to [[@new-york|New York]] in a box. Weeks later, tiny spiders hatched and spun threads all over his dresser.

Many people are scared of spiders. White wanted readers to see them differently. The book describes Charlotte's work accurately. There is the sticky spiral, the dry spokes, the way she wraps her prey in silk, and the egg sac she spins at the end of summer.

Real orb-weaving spiders like Charlotte are useful garden helpers, catching flies, mosquitoes and other [[@insects-importance|insects]]. Barn spiders usually live for about a year. Like Charlotte, many females lay a sac of hundreds of eggs in autumn and die before winter. The babies hatch in spring and float away on threads of silk, a trick called ballooning.

sec.h: A sad ending, and a hopeful one
sec.t:
Charlotte dies at the end of the book, alone at the fair, after saving Wilbur. Many readers cry. White did not soften it, but he did not leave it there either. Wilbur carries her egg sac home, and in spring her babies hatch. Most float away, but three stay as his friends.

The book won a Newbery Honor in 1953 and is often listed among the best-selling children's paperbacks ever. White ends it with a line about Charlotte that many readers know by heart. He wrote that it is not often someone comes along who is a true friend and a good writer, and Charlotte was both.

text: The Quran is the holy book of Islam. Muslims believe it is the word of God (Allah in Arabic), revealed to the Prophet Muhammad through the angel Jibril, known in English as Gabriel, over about 23 years. It is written in Arabic and has 114 chapters, called surahs.

For about 2 billion Muslims around the world, the Quran is a guide for faith and daily life. It speaks about God and about the prophets who came before Muhammad, such as Ibrahim (Abraham), Musa (Moses) and Isa (Jesus). It also teaches about honesty, prayer, charity, justice and kindness to parents, orphans and strangers.

st.prompt: According to Muslim tradition, what was the first word revealed to the Prophet Muhammad?

Salaam, meaning "peace"
Allah, meaning "God"

st.reveal: Muslims believe the first revelation began with the word Iqra, meaning "read" or "recite". The word "Quran" itself comes from the same Arabic root and means "the recitation", because it was first passed on aloud.

sec.h: How the Quran came to be
sec.t:
According to Muslim belief, the first revelation came in about 610 CE, when Muhammad was meditating in a cave called Hira on a mountain near Mecca. The angel told him "*Iqra*", meaning "Read!" or "Recite". Revelations continued for the rest of his life, in Mecca and later in Medina.

His companions memorised the verses and wrote them on whatever they had: parchment, palm leaves, flat bones. After his death in 632 CE, the first caliph, Abu Bakr, had them gathered together. Around 650 CE, the third caliph, Uthman, had standard copies made and sent to major cities. The text Muslims read today follows that version.

India has one of the largest Muslim populations in the world, and the Quran has been translated into many Indian languages, including Urdu, Malayalam, Tamil, Bengali, Gujarati and Hindi. Old handwritten copies, some decorated with gold, are kept in libraries such as the Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Library in Patna and the Raza Library in Rampur.

Each surah has a name, often taken from a word inside it, like *Al-Baqarah* (The Cow) or *Maryam* (Mary). After the short opening chapter, the surahs are arranged roughly from longest to shortest, not in the order they were revealed. The longest has 286 verses. The shortest has just three.

The opening chapter, *Al-Fatiha*, has seven verses. Muslims recite it in every unit of their daily prayers, which means many people say it at least 17 times a day. Almost every surah begins with the words *Bismillah ir-Rahman ir-Rahim*, "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful".

Because the Quran is so honoured, writing it out became an art. Islamic religious art usually avoids pictures of people, so calligraphers made the words themselves beautiful, in flowing or angular styles of [[@arabic-script|Arabic script]]. Verses decorate mosques from Spain to India, including the gateways of the Taj Mahal, where the letters grow larger near the top so that they look the same size from the ground.

Muslims treat printed copies with care. Many wash before touching one, keep it on a high shelf and never place it on the floor. Translations exist in more than 100 languages. Most Muslims see them as explanations of the meaning, while the Arabic text is considered the Quran itself. Its teachings shape festivals like [[@eid|Eid]] and the pilgrimage to [[@mecca-hajj|Mecca]], which millions of Muslims make every year.
